title: Why tests flake
summary: A flaky test passes and fails on the same code. The usual causes, read from a real repeat-run report, and a time-of-day test made deterministic.

steps.title: Same commit, different result
body: A **flaky** test passes and fails without any change to the code. One flaky test in a suite of 3,000 is enough to teach a team to press "re-run" instead of reading failures, and then real failures get re-run too.
Below are 20 CI runs of the same commit. Pick a row to see why it behaves that way. The causes are always some input the test does not control:
- **time**: `DateTime.Now`, time zones, daylight saving, month ends, and timing (`Task.Delay(100)` "should be enough");
- **order and shared state**: static fields, a shared database, files in a fixed folder: tests that pass alone and fail together;
- **async and concurrency**: missing `await`, races between a background worker and the assertion;
- **environment**: culture (`1.234,50` on a German agent), the machine's time zone, available ports, CPU speed;
- **the outside world**: real HTTP calls, DNS, a shared staging service.

testviz.title: 20 runs of commit 3f2a9c1 on CI
testviz.subtitle: green passed, red failed, grey skipped

tests.name: OrderTests.Total_includes_vat
tests.cause: Deterministic: only its own inputs. This is what every test should look like.

tests.name: GreetingTests.Says_good_morning
tests.cause: Reads the real clock. The failing runs started after noon UTC. Fix: pass a `FakeTimeProvider` set to 09:00.

tests.name: ExportTests.Writes_csv
tests.cause: Writes to `C:\temp\export.csv`, and another test (or another CI job on the same agent) reads or deletes it at the same time. Fix: a temp folder per test.

tests.name: OutboxTests.Sends_all_messages
tests.cause: Waits `Task.Delay(50)` for a background worker; on a busy agent the worker needs 60 ms. Fix: await the worker's completion signal (`DrainAsync`), never a guess.

tests.name: IdTests.First_id_is_1
tests.cause: Uses a `static` id counter that other tests also call; it fails whenever another test ran first. Fix: an instance per test, or reset state in the constructor.

tests.name: InvoiceTests.Formats_total
tests.cause: Not flaky in the usual sense: runs 11-20 went to a new agent pool with culture de-DE, where `12.5m.ToString("0.00")` is `12,50`. Fix: format with `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture`, and test under another culture on purpose.

steps.prompt: Match each flaky symptom to its most likely cause.
pairs: fails only when the whole suite runs, passes alone
shared state between tests (a static field, a shared table)
fails only in the evening runs
the test reads the real clock
fails one run in twenty, more often on busy agents
a fixed delay waiting for async work
fails on every run on the new build agents
the agents' culture or time zone
fails when the staging API is being deployed
a real network call in a test

steps.prompt: Your team adds automatic retries: a failed test is re-run up to 3 times before CI goes red. What is the main risk?
options: Real intermittent bugs (races, timeouts) in the product are hidden as well, and the flaky tests are never fixed
Retries make the suite slower on green runs
Retries do not work with xUnit
Nothing: a passing retry proves the code works
steps.explain: A race that fails one time in twenty in a test may fail one time in twenty for customers. Retries are acceptable as a short, visible quarantine (and the MTP retry extension reports them), never as the fix.

steps.title: Make the greeting test deterministic
prompt: This test passed for months and now fails some evenings. It mirrors the code's logic and reads the real clock:
var expected = DateTime.Now.Hour < 12 ? "Good morning" : DateTime.Now.Hour < 18 ? "Good afternoon" : "Good evening";
It is flaky (two clock reads straddle 11:59:59.999) and it tests nothing: any bug in the code is copied into `expected`. The code, compiled beside your tests:
// In the user's local time: morning until 12:00, afternoon until 18:00, then evening.
return hour < 12 ? "Good morning" : hour < 18 ? "Good afternoon" : "Good evening";

Replace it with `public class GreetingTests`: at least **5** tests with a `FakeTimeProvider` set to fixed moments (11:59 and 12:00, 17:59 and 18:00 ...), and **one** with a local time zone that is not UTC (`clock.SetLocalTimeZone(...)`). Four planted bugs.
starter: var expected = DateTime.Now.Hour < 12 ? "Good morning" : DateTime.Now.Hour < 18 ? "Good afternoon" : "Good evening";
solution: static FakeTimeProvider At(int hour, int minute) => new(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 11, 27, hour, minute, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));
public void Greets_by_the_hour(int hour, int minute, string expected) => Assert.Equal(expected, Greeting.For(At(hour, minute)));
var clock = At(9, 0);   // 09:00 UTC is 14:00 at UTC+5

target: return hour < 12 ? "Good morning" : hour < 18 ? "Good afternoon" : "Good evening";

mutants.name: it uses UTC instead of the user's time
mutants.hint: FakeTimeProvider's local time zone is UTC by default: set another one with SetLocalTimeZone.

require.message: One test sets a local time zone that is not UTC

hints: A helper builds a clock at a given time: `new FakeTimeProvider(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 11, 27, hour, minute, 0, TimeSpan.Zero))`.
Test both sides of each boundary: 11:59 and 12:00, 17:59 and 18:00.

For the time zone: `clock.SetLocalTimeZone(TimeZoneInfo.CreateCustomTimeZone("Test+5", TimeSpan.FromHours(5), "Test+5", "Test+5"))`, then 09:00 UTC is afternoon. A custom zone does not depend on the machine's time zone database.
steps.explain: Fixed inputs make the test deterministic, and writing the expected greeting by hand makes it actually test something. The time-zone case is the one people forget, and the one that fails on servers set to UTC.
